newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Thousands flock to see Cyprus weeping icon.
newsitem.headline: Thousands flock to see Cyprus weeping icon.

text.p: People on the Mediterranean island of Cyprus are flocking to see a handful of religious icons that believers say are shedding tears and the Greek Orthodox church says is a divine omen.

A centuries-old icon of Virgin Mary pressing to her face the hand of baby Jesus has drawn more than 20,000 people since the traces of tears were noticed flowing from the Virgin's right eye down her red robe.

"It's a miracle," murmured a woman dressed in black kneeling in front of the 15th or 16th Century painting cast in a silver and gold frame and kept at the 10th Century Kykkos Monastery, a 90-minute drive from Nicosia in the Troodos mountains.
"This is where Jesus wept," said a policeman standing next to the icon, tracing a line down the painting where colour was faded.
Monastery officials say that in the beginning of February a young novice saw that the icon had started to weep.

Since then claims of weeping icons, heralded by the Greek Orthodox Church of Cyprus as a "divine omen", have been reported from the village of Mammari, 20 km (12 miles) west of Nicosia and at a church in the Nicosia suburb of Strovolos.

Belief in miracles associated with icons -- weeping, bleeding or instant cures -- is not uncommon in Cyprus, which boasts a church tracing its lineage back to Christ's first companions, known to Christians as the Apostles.
While weeping icons of Virgin Mary are not uncommon, a weeping Jesus is, prompting debate of what it all means, said theologist Demetrios Athanassoulas.

"There are two options. It could mean the Holy Virgin is seeking the prayers of the people to God in addition to Her own and their repentance, or it could be a warning of a calamity," he told Reuters.
Some believers have associated the phenomenon with a severe drought currently afflicting Cyprus. Others have connected it to the ongoing stalemate in what is known as the "national issue".

Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkish troops invaded after Greek Cypriots staged a coup backed by the military then ruling Greece. The northern third of the island is occupied by some 30,000 Turkish soldiers.
